## Living+
"Living+" is the sixth episode of the fourth season of the American satirical comedy-drama television series Succession, and the 35th episode overall. It was written by Georgia Pritchett and Will Arbery and directed by Lorene Scafaria, and originally aired on HBO on April 30, 2023.
Succession centers on the Roy family, the owners of global media and entertainment conglomerate Waystar RoyCo, and their fight for control of the company amidst uncertainty about the health of the family's patriarch Logan (Brian Cox), who has passed away by this point of the series. The episode sees the Roys preparing the launch of "Living+", Logan's unrealized initiative on Waystar's Investor Day, as the ambition of Kendall (Jeremy Strong) and the unresolved grief of Roman (Kieran Culkin) threaten to destabilize the company. The episode notably features Cox's first appearance since Logan's death three episodes prior in "Connor's Wedding", as Logan appears via videos he had recorded for the launch.
“Living+" received critical acclaim, with praise for the performances (especially from Strong, Sarah Snook and Matthew Macfadyen), direction, and satirical elements. The episode earned Primetime Emmy Award nominations...

## New product development
In business and engineering, new product development (NPD) or simply product development is the complete process of bringing a new product to market. Product development also includes renewing an existing product and introducing a product into a new market. New product development is the realization of a market opportunity by making a product available for purchase. The products developed by a commercial organization provide the means to generate income. A central aspect of NPD is product design.
Many technology-intensive organizations exploit technological innovation in a rapidly changing consumer market. A product can be a tangible asset or good or intangible services or user experiences. NPD requires an understanding of customer needs and wants, the competitive environment, and the nature of the market.
Cost, time, and quality are the main variables that drive customer needs. Aiming at these three variables, innovative companies develop continuous practices and strategies to better satisfy customer requirements and to increase their own market share by regular development of new products. There are many uncertainties and challenges which companies must face throughout the process.

## Marketing communications
Marketing communications (also known MC, marcom(s), marcomm(s) or just simply communications) refers to the combined use of different marketing channels and tools. Marketing communication channels focus on how businesses communicate a message to their desired market, or the greater market in general. It can also include the internal communications of the organization. Marketing communication tools include advertising, personal selling, direct marketing, sponsorship, communication, public relations, social media, customer journey, and promotion.
MC are made up of the marketing mix which is made up of the 4 Ps (Price, Promotion, Place and Product), for a business selling goods, and made up of 7 Ps: Price, Promotion, Place, Product, People, Physical evidence and Process, for a service-based business.

## Content marketing
Content marketing is a form of marketing focused on creating, publishing, and distributing content for a targeted audience online. It is often used to achieve the following business goals: attract attention and generate leads, expand their customer base, generate or increase online sales, increase brand awareness or credibility, and engage a community of online users. Content marketing attracts new customers by creating and sharing valuable free content as well as by helping companies create sustainable brand loyalty, providing valuable information to consumers, and creating a willingness to purchase products from the company in the future.
Content marketing starts with identifying the customer's needs. After that, the information can be presented in a variety of long form and short form formats, including news, video, white papers, e-books, infographics, email newsletters, case studies, podcasts, how-to guides, question and answer articles, photos, blogs, etc. Examples of short form content include short blog posts and social media posts.
Content marketing requires continuous delivery of large amounts of content, preferably within a content marketing strategy.

## Note-taking
Note-taking (sometimes written as notetaking or note taking) is the practice of recording information from different sources and platforms. By taking notes, the writer records the essence of the information, freeing their mind from having to recall everything. Notes are commonly drawn from a transient source, such as an oral discussion at a meeting, or a lecture (notes of a meeting are usually called minutes), in which case the notes may be the only record of the event. Since the advent of writing and literacy, notes traditionally were almost always handwritten (often in notebooks), but the introduction of notetaking software and websites has made digital notetaking possible and widespread. Note-taking is a foundational skill in personal knowledge management.

plan.title: Capture it once: meet your new note-taking app
plan.description: A launch video for a note-taking app that shows why notes matter and how capturing them frees your mind. It covers the move from notebooks to digital notes and how to start with your first note.

beats.narration: Your meeting ended ten minutes ago. Can you say what was decided? Memory fades fast, and nobody can replay a conversation.
For a lecture or a talk, your notes may be the only record that it ever happened. That is a lot to trust to memory.

props.text: Sometimes your notes are the only record of what happened.

beats.narration: Note-taking is the practice of recording information from different sources. You capture the essence, so your mind is free to listen.

props.definition: The practice of recording information from different sources, capturing its essence so you do not have to recall everything.

beats.narration: For a long time, notes were handwritten, usually in notebooks. Pages filled up. Pages got lost. Finding one idea meant flipping through them all.
Handwriting filled notebooks. Then software and websites arrived, and digital notes became widespread. Our app starts from that shift.
So here is the promise. Capture a thought quickly. Keep everything in one place. Find it again when it matters.
Capturing should be easy. You are in a meeting, a lecture or on a busy street, and the idea is safe before it slips away.

person typing on phone walking street
props.alt: person using phone and laptop at a cafe

beats.narration: Ideas move in a few steps. First you capture. Then you organize. Then you revisit, and ideas turn into something you can use.
Without notes, you recall fuzzy outlines, forgotten details, and your attention splits. With notes, details are saved and your mind is free.
Notes come from everywhere. Lectures. Meetings. Spoken conversations. Whatever the source, they belong in one place.
Meeting notes are usually called minutes. They keep a team on the same page, long after everyone has left the room.
Note-taking is a foundational skill in personal knowledge management. In plain words, it is how you build what you know.

props.text: Notes are how you build what you know.

beats.narration: Students use it to study. Professionals use it to prepare. Writers use it to catch the first rough spark of a story.

props.alt: students reading and writing in a library

beats.narration: Remember what matters: capture quickly, keep it organized, find it fast, and stay focused on the person in front of you.
We built this by starting with a need, not a feature list. Product development begins with understanding what people actually want.
Picture your next week. A class, a call, a project kickoff. Every important word captured, and none of it left to chance.

accuracy.reason: It makes no invented numbers or features, and the note-taking claims trace to the notes. The "Getting started takes a minute" claim and the "find it fast" promise are unsupported, and the diagram presents the history as a strict linear chain.

coverage.reason: It is mostly a generic essay on note-taking. It has no concrete product features (sync, search, platforms, pricing), no placeholders, no named app, and no real call to action such as a download or link.

structure.reason: The chapters are clear, but the history section is long for a launch video. Beats 9-11 repeat the capture/keep/find idea and the meetings/lectures point, and the product pitch arrives late.

hook_ending.reason: The opener, "Your meeting ended ten minutes ago. Can you say what was decided?", is a strong hook. The ending line is decent but is a recap with no call to action.

tone.reason: The voice is warm, conversational and suited to a general US audience. It leans slightly toward explainer rather than launch excitement.

visuals.reason: The scene types vary well (clips, diagram, versus, steps, checklist), and the queries fit the narration. There is no app UI or screenshot placeholder, and the diagram and versus are a bit filler.

originality.reason: It is generic and repeats the Wikipedia definition. Lines like "Product development begins with understanding what people actually want" are filler that fits any product.

instructions.reason: It is a launch video of about the right length, with a problem-solution arc. It lacks a product name, differentiators and a call to action, and it spends time on a textbook definition.

language.reason: The prose is fluent, with short punchy sentences. It has a few stiff textbook phrases such as "Spoken conversations" and "Meeting notes are usually called minutes".
